extracted.intended_audience: Technology Center Directors; Patent Examining Corps; patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on applying and making rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (indefiniteness), including when claim terms lack clear definition or proper antecedent basis and what analyses, examples, and procedural steps to include in office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of definiteness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the definiteness requirement for claim language is to ensure that the scope of the claims is clear so that the public is informed of the boundaries of what constitutes infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this policy objective to guide whether claim language is sufficiently clear; focus on public notice of claim boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard (person of ordinary skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are found indefinite only where a person of ordinary skill in the art could not determine the metes and bounds of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a POSITA would be able to ascertain claim scope; if POSITA would read a claim with more than one reasonable interpretation, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a claim its broadest reasonable interpretation, and review the claim as a whole in light of the specification (other claims and the written description) as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not analyze claim terms in a vacuum; consider the application disclosure, teachings of the prior art, and claim interpretation by POSITA at time of invention (cites MPEP 2173.02, 2173.05(a), 2143.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of reasonable interpretations → rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the language of a claim, considered as a whole in light of the specification and given its broadest reasonable interpretation, is such that a person of ordinary skill would read it with more than one reasonable interpretation then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claim subject to more than one interpretation and at least one interpretation would render the claim unpatentable over the prior art, examiner should (1) reject the claim as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph, and (2) reject the claim over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the prior art applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function limitation without corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a means-plus-function limitation without disclosing corresponding structure in the specification can be held indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify lack of corresponding structure in spec for means/step-plus-function language (see Halliburton/Biomedino examples); if absent, 112 second paragraph rejection appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric limitation lacking disclosed measurement method
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that includes a numeric limitation without disclosing which of multiple methods of measuring that number should be used may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple reasonable measurement methods exist and spec doesn't indicate which to use, consider 112 second paragraph rejection (see Honeywell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective or purely opinion-dependent terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of terms that are completely dependent on a person's subjective opinion can render a claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term's meaning turns entirely on subjective judgment and POSITA cannot ascertain boundaries, pursue an indefiniteness rejection (see Datamize).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is unclear whether a particular limitation refers to an element previously presented, a claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph as being indefinite for failing to point out and distinctly claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject where antecedent basis is missing and scope is not reasonably ascertainable; provide constructive suggestions for correction. Rarely, lack of explicit antecedent basis may not render claim indefinite if reasonably ascertainable (see Energizer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term not used/defined in specification and not discernible
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim term is not used or defined in the specification and the meaning of the claim term is not discernible, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph would be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If term is not used/defined but meaning is discernible by POSITA, do not make a 112 rejection; instead make an objection under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) to the specification for lack of support/antecedent basis (example: 'surrender value protected investment credits' was discernible and not indefinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-defined terms (lexicographer) must still be clear to POSITA
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may define claim terms in the written description and be their own lexicographers, but the provided definition must itself be clear and precise to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a definition is given in spec, if that definition's broadest reasonable interpretation results in more than one meaning, an indefiniteness rejection is appropriate; check for inconsistencies between claim and specification disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should not use per se rules for technical rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections; examiners should not be interpreted as discouraged from making appropriate 112 second paragraph rejections when evidence exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blanket/formulaic rejections; examine context. Examples: minor wording changes (use of 'the' vs 'a') when claim otherwise clear should not be a per se rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explanatory analysis in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph should include an analysis as to why the language, phrase(s) and term(s) used render the claim vague and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how and why claim language is unclear; provide examples and reasoning to help applicant respond; if withdrawal of rejection occurs after traversal, explain what prompted change citing specific argument or authority; if traversal not persuasive, maintain rejection and explain why not persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive suggestions to correct antecedent problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should make constructive suggestions as to how to correct any antecedence problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing a 112 rejection for antecedent basis, propose amendments or clarifications (see provided examples illustrating how antecedent issues arise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity from similarly worded multiple elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness may arise when a claim includes similarly worded structural elements and it is unclear whether recitations refer to the same or distinct elements (e.g., 'a translator controller' vs 'the linear translator').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ambiguous whether later recitation is same element or different, issue 112 second paragraph rejection; if initial phrasing had used clearer antecedent ('a translator controller' then 'the controller') the issue might not arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate definiteness by threshold of clarity and particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination should focus on whether the claims meet the threshold requirements of clarity and precision — whether the claims set out and describe a particular subject matter with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assess whether more suitable language exists; focus on whether claim language permits POSITA to determine scope with reasonable certainty.
